Hi there. What brings you in today?
I sprained my ankle on Tuesday. It is still swollen, and it has been hurting since then.
Can you walk on it? And have you been taking anything for the pain?
I can walk, but not far. I have been taking painkillers for two days, and they help for about four hours.
Understood. Any medicine you take regularly, or anything you are allergic to?
Nothing regular, and no allergies. Here is my passport and my insurance card. Do I need an appointment, or can I wait?
You can wait. It is about forty minutes. Your insurance covers the visit, and anything the doctor prescribes you buy at the drugstore next door.
That is fine, thank you. And could you tell me roughly what the visit will cost, so there is no surprise later?

I work the front desk at an urgent care clinic, and I hear about eighty people a day. Here is the honest truth: the first thirty seconds decide how fast you are seen, and most visitors from abroad use those thirty seconds badly. They apologise, they explain that their English is not good, and they tell me the story from the beginning of the holiday. I do not need any of that. I need three things, in this order. What is wrong, where, and how long it has been going on. My ankle has been hurting since Tuesday. That single sentence tells me more than four minutes of story. Then, if there is anything I should know, say it in one line: I take medicine for my blood pressure, or I am allergic to something. And finally, have your insurance card and your passport in your hand before you reach me. Not in the bag, in your hand. Nobody is judging your grammar here. We are triaging a waiting room.

A quick word about buying medicine in another country, because travellers get this wrong in both directions. In the United States, a lot of things you are used to buying over the counter still need a prescription, and a lot of things that need a prescription at home are simply on the shelf. So do not assume either way. Walk into the drugstore, go to the counter at the back, and ask the pharmacist directly. They are allowed to advise you, they do it all day, and it is free. Say what the problem is and what you normally take at home, and ask whether there is something similar. Two more things. Take a photograph of the box of anything you take regularly, because the brand name changes from country to country and the ingredient does not. And keep every receipt, because if you claim on your travel insurance later, the receipt is the only thing they will actually look at.
